paras: The killing of Sam Moore and threatened lynching of Lawson Adams took place at Gadsden, Alabama, on December 9, 1888, when Moore, described as a Black man accused of a killing, was killed while resisting arrest and Adams, jailed as his supposed accomplice, was expected to be lynched. Wire reports said a mob had gathered at Gadsden and that troops had been asked for, but no report of what became of Adams was found. Papers across the country carried the story in the same days as the Birmingham jail riot, some under headlines that looked ahead to a lynching.
According to a special dispatch to the Chattanooga Times, Sam Moore, "a negro," had killed a man on Saturday night, December 8. The dispatch did not name the man he was accused of killing.

On Sunday morning, Deputy Sheriffs A. C. Christian and Al Herzberg went out to "the new furnace" to arrest Moore, but he had fled. Both deputies were shot and wounded there by what the dispatch called "unknown parties." Officers then arrested Lawson Adams, "supposed to be an accomplice of Moore," and locked him in jail.

Moore was later "found and killed for resisting arrest," in the dispatch's words; it did not say who killed him. The dispatch closed with the belief that Adams would "be lynched before morning," and a California brief the next day said a mob at Gadsden threatened to lynch him. A Birmingham dispatch of December 10 reported news from Gadsden of a mob there to lynch a Black man, adding that troops had been requested and might be sent that night.
No report was found of whether troops reached Gadsden, whether the mob attacked the jail, or what became of Adams. Nor does the coverage show an inquest into Moore's death.

The Chattanooga Times special ran on December 10 in the Savannah Morning News under "Lynching Looked For," in the Los Angeles Daily Herald as "More Lynching in Prospect," and in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union as "Southern Lawlessness." Through mid-December, weeklies in Ohio and Kentucky reprinted it as "Murderer Killed by Officers," treating Moore's guilt as settled, and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer's condensed version called him "a negro murderer" and left out the lynching prediction.

In the Newberry Herald and News the Gadsden mob appeared as a short paragraph headed "More Lynching" inside a long Birmingham roundup on the riot at the Birmingham jail. No account in the coverage questioned the killing of Moore or gave any version from Moore's or Adams' side.

The two independent reports differ on the accusation: the Chattanooga special said Moore had killed "a man" and that the deputies were wounded, while the Birmingham item said the mob's target had "killed a policeman." The Gadsden-datelined special names those involved and is the more detailed source, while the Birmingham item passed on secondhand "news from Gadsden."

reader.title: Killing of Sam Moore and threatened lynching of Lawson Adams
bases: The coverage centers on a mob expected or said to be gathering at Gadsden to lynch a jailed man, Lawson Adams, after deputies were shot and Sam Moore was killed resisting arrest (A2, A6, A9).

The papers report only a threatened lynching of Adams, who was in jail when the coverage ends, and no report says he was killed (A2, A6, A9); Moore was 'killed for resisting arrest' by unnamed captors in the course of an arrest, with no mob described (A2).

A Chattanooga Times special from Gadsden (A2) and a separate Birmingham dispatch (A9) agree that a Black man accused of a killing was the target of a lynch mob at Gadsden on about Dec. 9-10, though they differ on who was killed (see conflicts).

accounts.label: Chattanooga Times special from Gadsden
accounts.gist: Deputies going to arrest Sam Moore for a Saturday-night killing were shot and wounded by unknown parties; Lawson Adams was jailed as an accomplice; Moore was found and killed resisting arrest; Adams was expected to be lynched before morning.

accounts.label: Birmingham dispatch, Dec. 10
accounts.gist: News from Gadsden said a mob was there to lynch 'a negro who killed a policeman yesterday', and troops had been asked for.

framing.detail: The Chattanooga special ran with headlines anticipating a lynching ('Lynching Looked For', 'More Lynching in Prospect') and stated Moore's guilt and the killing as justified ('killed for resisting arrest').
Later country-paper copies ran it as 'Murderer Killed by Officers', and the Seattle condensation called Moore 'a negro murderer'.
The Birmingham roundup placed the Gadsden mob under 'More Lynching' as a coda to the Birmingham jail riot.

versions.value: Moore killed 'a man' Saturday night; the deputies sent to arrest him were wounded, not killed.
The mob's target was 'a negro who killed a policeman yesterday'.

conflicts.note: The Chattanooga special, datelined Gadsden and giving names, is the more detailed source; the Birmingham paragraph is secondhand ('There comes news from Gadsden') and may have conflated the wounding of the deputies with a killing.

versions.value: Lawson Adams, jailed as Moore's supposed accomplice.
An unnamed 'negro' said to have killed a policeman.

conflicts.note: Moore had already been killed by the time the Chattanooga special was sent, so its mob target is Adams; the Birmingham item names no one.
